title: Surveying and levelling
summary: Surveying questions divide into three kinds: definitions and instrument names, a handful of formulas, and error-elimination rules. The formulas are few enough to memorise outright — Ks + C, 1719/D, 0.0673d², BB − FB = 180°. The error rules are where marks are actually won and lost, so learn which technique removes which error, and which error nothing removes. Throughout, the organising idea is the same one that opens the subject: work from whole to part, so errors are localised rather than accumulated.

sections.heading: Principles, classification and chain surveying
sections.body:
**The fundamental principle is to work from whole to part.** A small number of **control points** are established to high accuracy over the whole area, and only then is detail filled in between them.

**Why this order.** Survey errors **accumulate**. Measuring detail from one point to the next carries each small error into the next measurement, so the total grows without bound. Fixing an accurate framework first means:

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| Errors are **localised** | A mistake in detail affects only that detail |
| Errors are **contained**, not accumulated | Each part ties into already-correct control |
| Work can proceed **independently** | Several parties can survey at once |
| A blunder is **detectable** | Detail must close onto known control |

That last row is the practical value: working from whole to part builds a **check** into every stage. Working from part to whole offers no check until the very end, when it is too late.

**The second principle:** to fix a point relative to two known points, at least **two independent measurements** are required — two distances, two angles, or one of each. Hence trilateration (two distances), triangulation (two angles), polar coordinates (one of each — what a total station does), and perpendicular offsets.

A **well-conditioned triangle** applies the same idea to shape: no angle smaller than about **30°** nor larger than **120°**, because a point fixed by two nearly parallel rays is poorly determined. The ideal is near-equilateral.

**Classification** of surveys: by **instrument** (chain, compass, plane table, theodolite, tacheometric, photogrammetric, GNSS); by **purpose** (topographic, cadastral, engineering, hydrographic, geological, military); by **whether earth curvature is considered** — **plane** surveying ignores it (areas under about 250 km²), **geodetic** accounts for it.

**Chain surveying** operations, whose names are examined:

| Operation | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Ranging** | **Fixing intermediate points on the line** |
| **Chaining** | Measuring length along it |
| **Offsetting** | Measuring detail perpendicular (or oblique) to the line |
| Standardising | Checking the chain, which **stretches** with use |

**Ranging** matters because if an intermediate point strays off the line, the measured path is a **zig-zag**, and the sum of its parts is **always longer** than the straight distance — a systematic error, always in the same direction, which cannot cancel out. **Direct** ranging is used when the ends are mutually visible; **indirect (reciprocal)** ranging when they are not, two surveyors aligning each other alternately until they converge onto the line.

**Chain corrections.** For a chain of wrong length:

> **True length = measured length × (incorrect chain length / true chain length)**

So a chain that has **stretched** gives measurements that are **too small**, and correcting makes them larger. The same ratio applies to **areas as its square** and **volumes as its cube** — forgetting to square it for an area is the commonest error in the topic.

Other corrections: **slope** (always subtractive), **temperature**, **pull**, **sag** (for a suspended tape, always subtractive). Slope and sag can only shorten the true horizontal distance.

sections.heading: Compass surveying and bearings
sections.body:
**Two bearing systems** exist because they serve different purposes. The **whole circle bearing (WCB)** runs **0° to 360° clockwise from north** and is used by the **prismatic compass** and by all computation, because trigonometry needs a single continuous number. The **quadrantal or reduced bearing (RB)** is used by the **surveyor's compass** and in older records, and is more readable to a human.

**The conversion, quadrant by quadrant** — the table to carry:

| WCB | Quadrant | Reduced bearing | Measured from |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0° – 90°** | I — **NE** | **RB = WCB** | **N toward E** |
| **90° – 180°** | II — **SE** | **RB = 180° − WCB** | **S toward E** |
| **180° – 270°** | III — **SW** | **RB = WCB − 180°** | **S toward W** |
| **270° – 360°** | IV — **NW** | **RB = 360° − WCB** | **N toward W** |

The pattern that makes it memorable: quadrants **I and III** subtract nothing and 180° and are measured the natural way, while **II and IV** subtract the WCB from 180° and 360°. The prefix alternates **N, S, S, N** and the suffix runs **E, E, W, W**. So a WCB of 200° is **S 20° W**.

**Kinds of bearing:**

| Bearing | Reference |
|---|---|
| **True bearing** | **True (geographic) north** |
| **Magnetic bearing** | **Magnetic north** — differs by the **declination** |
| Arbitrary | Any convenient direction |
| **Fore bearing (FB)** | In the direction of progress |
| **Back bearing (BB)** | Back along the same line |

> **BB = FB ± 180°** — **+** when FB < 180°, **−** when FB > 180°
> **True bearing = magnetic bearing + declination** (east positive, west negative)

Declination changes slowly with time and place, so a magnetic bearing must always be recorded with the **date** — an old plan's magnetic bearings cannot be reused without correction.

**Local attraction** is detected when **BB − FB ≠ 180°** beyond the permissible instrumental error. Then at least one of the two stations is disturbed.

Note what local attraction is **not**: the magnetic bearing **always** differs from the true bearing by the declination, everywhere on earth. That is normal and predictable. Local attraction is a **local** disturbance superimposed on it.

Causes: **iron and steel objects** (rails, pipes, poles, wire fences, reinforced concrete), **iron ore** in the ground, **electric current**, and — worth taking seriously — **the surveyor's own equipment**: a steel tape or chain laid beside the tripod, keys, spectacles, a phone.

**How to correct it.** Find a line whose FB and BB **do** differ by exactly 180°: **both** its stations are clean, so their bearings are correct. Work outward from that line. At each disturbed station the **error is the same for every bearing observed from it**, because the needle is deflected by one fixed amount there whatever the direction sighted. That single fact is what makes the correction possible.

Remedies in order of preference: **shift the station** away from the disturbance; apply the correction; or use a **theodolite** and measure **angles**, which does not depend on magnetism at all. The third is why modern practice has largely abandoned the compass for precise work.

sections.heading: Levelling
sections.body:
**Terms:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Back sight (BS)** | The **first** reading after setting up — on a point of known RL |
| **Fore sight (FS)** | The **last** reading before moving the instrument |
| **Intermediate sight (IS)** | Any reading between them |
| **Change point** | A point on which both an FS and a BS are taken |
| **Height of instrument (HI)** | RL of the line of collimation = RL + BS |
| **Reduced level (RL)** | Elevation above the datum |

**Two reduction methods**, and the choice is a real trade-off:

| | **Height of collimation** | **Rise and fall** |
|---|---|---|
| Computation | RL = HI − staff reading | RL = previous RL ± (rise or fall) |
| Speed | **Faster** | Slower |
| Intermediate sights | **NOT checked** | **Fully checked** |
| Suits | **Many intermediate sights** — profile and cross-section levelling | **Precise** work, fly levelling |
| Checks available | 2 | **3** |

**The arithmetic checks:**

> Height of collimation: **ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL**
> Rise and fall: **ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL**

The middle term is the whole point. The collimation method computes intermediate levels directly from the plane of collimation, so they never enter the sum and an arithmetic error in one **passes undetected**. The rise-and-fall method computes each level from the one before it, so every reading enters ΣRise − ΣFall and any error breaks the check.

**The rule for rise or fall** is reversed from intuition: if the **later** staff reading is **smaller**, the ground has **risen** (the staff is higher, so less of it is above the line of sight); if **larger**, the ground has **fallen**.

**Benchmarks**, in descending order of authority:

| Type | Established by | Datum |
|---|---|---|
| **GTS** (Great Trigonometrical Survey) | **National survey department** | **Mean sea level**, precisely determined |
| **Permanent** | Government or reliable agencies | Referred to a GTS benchmark |
| **Temporary (TBM)** | The **surveyor**, at the end of a day's work | Referred to the nearest permanent BM |
| **Arbitrary** | The surveyor | **Assumed** — commonly 100.000 m |

A **temporary** benchmark has a *correct* value tied into the national network; an **arbitrary** one has an invented value. Arbitrary levels are internally consistent but cannot be compared with anyone else's — adequate for setting out one building, useless for a scheme connecting to a road or drain elsewhere. **Mean sea level** is used because it is a single physical surface available to everyone.

Nepal's network is maintained by the **Survey Department**. The **2015 Gorkha earthquake** displaced control points across central Nepal, so benchmarks in the affected region had to be re-established.

**Curvature and refraction:**

> **Curvature alone = 0.0785 d²** m (makes objects appear **lower**)
> **Refraction restores about 1/7** of it (makes them appear **higher**)
> **Combined correction = 0.0673 d²** m, with d in **km**

Under a millimetre at 100 m, but **67 mm at 1 km** — which is why balancing back and fore sight distances is normally sufficient, and why **reciprocal levelling** is needed only for long sights.

**Reciprocal levelling** restores the cancellation by symmetry in time rather than space: read from near A, then from near B, and take the **mean** of the two apparent differences. Each setup has one short and one long sight, so errors that scale with distance enter with **opposite sign**. It removes **curvature, refraction and collimation** error; it does **not** remove staff graduation error or a non-level instrument.

**Special methods:** simple/differential (fly) levelling, **reciprocal** (wide obstacle), **profile** (along a line), **cross-section** (across it, for earthwork), **precise**, **trigonometric** (from vertical angles), check levelling. Permissible misclosure for ordinary work is commonly **± 12√K mm**, K in kilometres.

**The discipline underlying all of it:** keep BS and FS distances equal, **begin and end on a benchmark**, and never accept a run that has not closed. A run that does not close proves nothing about its own accuracy.

sections.heading: Theodolite, traversing and their errors
sections.body:
**Temporary adjustments** at each setup: **setting up** over the station, **centring** (plumb bob or optical plummet), **levelling** with the foot screws, and **focusing** eyepiece then objective to remove **parallax**. Parallax — the image not lying in the plane of the cross-hairs — causes a reading error that varies with the observer's eye position.

**Permanent adjustments**, in the order tested:

1. The **plate bubble axis** perpendicular to the vertical axis.
2. The **line of collimation** perpendicular to the trunnion axis.
3. The **trunnion axis** perpendicular to the vertical axis.
4. The **altitude bubble axis** parallel to the line of collimation.

**Which technique removes which error** — the heart of the topic:

| Error | Eliminated by |
|---|---|
| **Collimation** (sight not ⟂ trunnion axis) | **Both faces** — average FL and FR |
| **Trunnion axis** error | **Both faces** |
| Vertical index error | Both faces |
| **Eccentricity of centres** | Reading **both verniers** (A and B) and averaging |
| **Imperfect graduation** | **Repetition** on different parts of the circle |
| Accidental reading errors | Repetition or reiteration |
| **Vertical axis not truly vertical** | **NOTHING** — the instrument must be levelled properly |

That last row is the one to carry. An out-of-plumb vertical axis is not removed by changing face, by reading both verniers, or by repetition. The only defence is careful levelling, checked in two perpendicular directions and re-checked after any movement.

**Improving an angle:** **repetition** turns the **same** angle several times, accumulating on the circle and dividing by the number of repetitions; **reiteration** observes **several** angles round the horizon and closes back on the first, detecting error by the **closure of the horizon**.

**Traversing.** Compute **latitude (L cos θ)** and **departure (L sin θ)** for each line; for a **closed** traverse both should sum to zero, and the residuals are the closing error components:

> **e = √[(ΣL)² + (ΣD)²]**,  **tan θ = ΣD / ΣL**

Express the accuracy as a **relative** error, e ÷ perimeter:

| Relative closing error | Standard |
|---|---|
| 1 in 300 – 600 | Compass traverse |
| 1 in 1000 – 3000 | Theodolite traverse |
| 1 in 5000 and better | Precise work |

**Two balancing rules**, and the choice is a statement about which instrument was used:

| Rule | Assumes | Correction ∝ | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bowditch (compass)** | Linear and angular errors **comparable** | **Length** of line | **Compass** traverse |
| **Transit** | **Angular** more precise than linear | **Latitude / departure** | **Theodolite** traverse |

A theodolite measures angles to seconds while a taped distance is far less certain, so the transit rule leaves bearings largely alone and adjusts lengths.

**A caution that matters more than the arithmetic.** Balancing **hides** error; it does not remove it. If the closing error exceeds the permissible limit, **re-observe**. A gross blunder — a transposed digit, a missed whole degree — produces a large misclosure, and spreading it smoothly corrupts every station instead of the one at fault. The **direction** of the closing error often points at the offending line.

Sign conventions: **northing positive, southing negative; easting positive, westing negative**. For a closed traverse ΣN = ΣS and ΣE = ΣW — simply the statement that the traverse returns to where it began.

sections.heading: Tacheometry, plane tabling and modern instruments
sections.body:
**Tacheometry** measures **distance and elevation together, without chaining**, from one setup.

> **D = (f/i)·s + (f + d) = K·s + C**

with **K = f/i** the **multiplying constant** (typically **100**) and **C = f + d** the **additive constant** (0 to 0.3 m). A multiplying constant of 100 is deliberate: an intercept of 1.235 m means 123.5 m, so the distance is read by shifting a decimal point.

Modern instruments are **anallatic** — an extra lens makes **C = 0** and the relation reduces to **D = 100 s**.

**Inclined sight, staff vertical:**

> **D = K s cos²θ + C cos θ**
> **V = K s (sin 2θ)/2 + C sin θ**
> **RL = RL of instrument axis + V − central hair reading**  (+V elevation, −V depression)

The **cos²θ** appears squared: one cosine reduces the intercept as seen obliquely, one projects the slope distance onto the horizontal.

**Why tacheometry exists:** where chaining is impossible or unsafe — **steep or broken hill country**, **across a river or ravine**, **marshy or wooded ground**, or where **rapid contouring** is needed. Its accuracy, roughly **1 in 500 to 1 in 1000**, is lower than careful chaining, so it is used for **detail and contouring, never the primary control** — the whole-to-part principle again. The constants are found in the field by reading intercepts at known distances and fitting D = Ks + C.

**Plane tabling** — four methods, distinguished by **what is being fixed**:

| Method | Fixes | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Radiation** | **Detail**, from **one** station | Rays drawn, distances **measured** |
| **Intersection** | **Detail**, from **two** stations | Rays from both; no distance measured |
| **Traversing** | A **series of stations** | Table set at each in turn |
| **Resection** | **The station itself** | Rays drawn **from** known plotted points back to the observer |

The first three fix **objects**; **resection fixes the observer**. Its methods: by a **back ray**, the **two-point problem**, and the **three-point problem** (solved by tracing paper, or graphically by **Lehmann's rules** using the triangle of error).

**The danger circle.** If the station lies on or near the **circle through the three known points**, the rays intersect at a common point for *any* orientation, so the position is **indeterminate**. Choose a station well inside or well outside it.

Plane tabling's merit is that **plotting is done in the field, in view of the ground** — nothing is omitted, no field book, no transcription errors, errors visible at once. Its limitation is decisive in modern practice: it produces only the plotted sheet, with **no recorded measurements** to re-plot at another scale or re-check later. Accessories: **alidade**, **trough compass**, spirit level, **U-fork**, drawing sheet. **Orientation** is by trough compass (quick, but subject to local attraction) or by a **back ray to a plotted point** (more reliable, always preferred).

**Curves.** The **degree of curve** D is the angle subtended by a standard chord:

> **sin(D/2) = (C/2)/R**, and for small D, **R ≈ 57.3 C / D**

| Standard chord | Constant |
|---|---|
| **30 m** | **R = 1719/D** — metric practice in Nepal and India |
| **20 m** | R = 1146/D |
| 100 ft (arc) | 5730/D |

Curve elements: **T = R tan(Δ/2)**, **L = πRΔ/180**, long chord 2R sin(Δ/2), apex distance R[sec(Δ/2) − 1], mid-ordinate R[1 − cos(Δ/2)].

**Rankine's method** sets out by deflection angles, **δ = 1718.9 C/R minutes** — the same 1719 rearranged. The **first and last sub-chords are shorter** than the standard chord and need their own deflection angles; forgetting this is the commonest setting-out error.

**Areas and volumes.** **Simpson's rule** fits a parabola through every three ordinates, so it needs an **even number of intervals — an odd number of ordinates**:

> **Area = (d/3)[first + last + 4(even ordinates) + 2(remaining odd)]**

The coefficients run **1, 4, 2, 4, 2 … 4, 1**. The **trapezoidal rule** assumes a straight boundary and accepts **any** number of ordinates. With an even number of ordinates, apply Simpson's to the odd portion and treat the last strip as a trapezium.

The volume analogues: **trapezoidal (average end area)** and the **prismoidal formula**, which is Simpson's rule applied to areas — the difference between them is the **prismoidal correction**, normally **subtractive**.

**Total station and GNSS.** A **total station measures horizontal angle, vertical angle and slope distance**; horizontal distance, level difference and coordinates are all **computed** from them. Its EDM measures the **phase difference** of a signal returned from a prism, to about **± (2 mm + 2 ppm)**. Its greatest practical gain is the **elimination of manual booking**, which was the source of a large share of classical survey errors.

**GNSS needs four satellites** for a three-dimensional fix, because there are **four unknowns**: X, Y, Z and the **receiver clock error**. Each satellite gives one **pseudo-range** = true range + c·Δt. Light travels 30 cm per nanosecond, so a one-microsecond clock error is a 300 m position error — solving for it from a fourth satellite is cheaper than an atomic clock in every receiver.

| Technique | Accuracy |
|---|---|
| Single-point (autonomous) | 5 – 15 m |
| **DGPS** | 1 – 3 m |
| **RTK** (carrier phase) | **1 – 5 cm** |
| **Static** post-processed | **Millimetres** |

**DOP (dilution of precision)** matters as much as the satellite count: satellites clustered in one part of the sky give a weak fix — the **well-conditioned triangle** principle again.

**Total station and GNSS are complements, not rivals**: one needs **line of sight**, the other **sky view**. And a caution on heights — GNSS gives **ellipsoidal** heights while levelling gives **orthometric** heights above the geoid, differing by the **geoid undulation**, which is large and variable across Nepal.

formulas.label: Chain correction
formulas.expression: True length = measured × (incorrect chain length / true chain length)
formulas.note: Area scales as the square of the ratio, volume as the cube. A stretched chain reads short.

formulas.label: Fore and back bearing
formulas.expression: BB = FB ± 180°   (+ when FB < 180°, − when FB > 180°)
formulas.note: A departure from 180° indicates local attraction at one of the two stations.

formulas.label: Levelling checks
formulas.expression: ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL
formulas.note: The middle term exists only in the rise and fall method, which is why it alone checks intermediate sights.

formulas.label: Curvature and refraction
formulas.expression: Curvature 0.0785 d²;  refraction ≈ 1/7 of it;  combined 0.0673 d²   (d in km)
formulas.note: 67 mm at 1 km. Eliminated by equal sight distances, or by reciprocal levelling across an obstacle.

formulas.label: Tacheometric distance (stadia)
formulas.expression: D = K s + C;  inclined: D = K s cos²θ + C cos θ,  V = K s (sin 2θ)/2
formulas.note: K = f/i = 100; C = 0 for an anallatic lens. Note cos SQUARED in the horizontal distance.

formulas.label: Traverse closing error
formulas.note: Bowditch distributes ∝ line length; transit ∝ latitude/departure. Re-observe if beyond the permissible limit.

formulas.label: Degree of curve
formulas.expression: R ≈ 57.3 C / D  →  1719/D for a 30 m chord, 1146/D for 20 m;  δ = 1718.9 C/R minutes
formulas.note: First and last sub-chords are shorter and need their own deflection angles.

formulas.label: Simpson's rule
formulas.note: Requires an even number of intervals, hence an ODD number of ordinates. Coefficients 1,4,2,4,…,4,1.
